Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst. The president of Cornell University says they must do better following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student in recent weeks alleging she was gang-raped at a frat house in 2024. And Piers Christian Wright has more.
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff says it's a defining moment for the university.
What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come.
He acknowledges mounting questions over Cornell's handling of the young woman's rape allegations and concerns about campus culture.
It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.
Cornell's president says the school's taking immediate action to strengthen sexual assault prevention and education and substance use resources, and will take a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life.
He also announced an outside review into Cornell's handling of the case. Christian Wright, NPR News.
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says he's considered retiring, and Piers Kerry Johnson reports on fresh interviews with the justice as he promotes his new book.
Justice Alito tells CBS News he's considered retiring from the court.
Alito, who's 76 years old, was appointed by President George W. Bush.
He's already served 20 years on the Supreme Court and written major decisions reversing the right to abortion and paring back the Voting Rights Act.
Any justice's decision to retire before 2028 could set off a political tug of war.
Senate Republicans famously refused to even meet with President Obama's nominee, Merrick Garland, because they said it was too close to an election.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
The Coast Guard says it's still trying to account for the six people who were on board a medical plane that crashed off Nantucket early yesterday.
The Gulfstream G-100 jet was traveling from Bermuda to Boston when air traffic control lost contact with it. Hal Connerney from member station WBUR in Boston has more.
The Coast Guard is located jet debris 20 miles off Nantucket, where Admiral Matt Lake describes the search as a rescue operation,
but did say they would continue to update the "next of kin" as the operation unfolds.
This is a large and demanding search area. Our crews are employing fixed-wing aircraft, helicopter, boats and cutters to search the area and will continue to evaluate all available information as our operation progresses.
Lake said they are working with Massachusetts officials to dispatch crafts equipped with sonar to scan the ocean floor.
The Coast Guard says they plan to search until they're confident they will not find any survivors.
For NPR News, I'm Paul Connerney in Boston.
And there's no word on the cause of that crash. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Days before the first anniversary of the Gaza ceasefire, new assessments by UN agencies are warning that basic humanitarian needs in Gaza are still far from resolved.
Medical supplies are waiting months for clearance, and food assistance is being cut as funding runs out. And Pearson Azbaba has more from Gaza.
The World Health Organization said Friday the approval process for medical supplies can last two and a half months for Israeli clearance.
And if the supplies are rejected, the process starts over.
Israeli authorities classify some restricted equipment as dual use, with potential military applications.
But the WHO disputes that characterization, noting many are standard medical supplies used globally.
Meanwhile, the World Food Program warns a funding shortfall is cutting the number of people receiving monthly food assistance to 600,000, down from 1.1 million.
That leaves two-thirds of Gaza's population in crisis-level hunger. And with winter approaching, the UN notes about 1.7 million people remain displaced, many without advocate shelter, water or sanitation.
Anas Baba, NPR News, Gaza.
In South Korea, authorities are trying to free a large grey shark from a canal, where it's been stuck for more than two weeks.
The shark, named Bukanji, after the North Port Park in the city of Busan, where he's stuck, is about 11 and a half feet long.
Officials have used water jets and nets trying to coast him back out to sea, but so far, he doesn't appear interested.
